hints: Look carefully at the table, it gives the mass of one chain or one haem group, but one whole haemoglobin is not made of just one of each.
Recall how many alpha chains, beta chains and haem groups are in one haemoglobin molecule, then add them up before dividing by 1000.
walkthrough:
**Recall what one haemoglobin is made of**

A haemoglobin molecule is a quaternary protein with four polypeptides: two alpha-globin chains and two beta-globin chains. Each of the four chains holds one haem group, so there are four haem groups in total.

**Add up the total mass in Da**

Do not just add the three numbers once. You need two of each globin and four haems:
$$Total = (2 \times 15126) + (2 \times 15868) + (4 \times 617)$$
$$Total = 30252 + 31736 + 2468 = 64456 \text{ Da}$$

**Convert Da to kDa**

There are $1000 \text{ Da}$ in $1 \text{ kDa}$, so divide by 1000:
$$Mass = \frac{64456}{1000} = 64.456 \text{ kDa} \approx 64.5 \text{ kDa}$$

options.A: This is $15126 + 15868 + 617 = 31611$ Da or 31.6 kDa, which is only one alpha, one beta and one haem, so only about half a molecule.
options.B: This is $15126 + 15868 + (4 \times 617) = 33462$ Da or 33.5 kDa, which is only one alpha and one beta with four haems, so still only half the protein part.
options.C: This is $(2 \times 15126) + (2 \times 15868) + 617 = 62605$ Da or 62.6 kDa, which correctly doubles the globins but only adds one haem group instead of four.
options.D: This correctly includes two alpha chains, two beta chains and four haem groups to give about 64.5 kDa for the whole haemoglobin molecule.
